question: The rules: who is allowed to do what, and is it law yet?
answer: This page reads every rule the library holds on U.S. crypto in one walk: the GENIUS Act (enacted July 18, 2025) and its 28 dated steps, 14 of them proposals not yet final; the 8 other crypto rules, orders and bills and where each stands; the Crypto Hub's nine-step legal process walk with its 7 worked cases and qualification records; the SEC's custody proposal provision by provision (36 provisions, all 760 pages and 342 comment questions); the CFTC's 30-provision baseline; the SEC's Innovation Exemption (12 conditions, 15 clocks); the Federal Reserve Board's two GENIUS proposals; and 9 other jurisdictions' laws. A proposal grants no permission to anyone until it is final.

rows.title: Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act)
fields: The Act takes effect on the earlier of January 18, 2027 (18 months after enactment) or 120 days after the primary regulators issue final implementing rules. No final rule existed by September 20, 2026 (120 days before January 18, 2027), so any later final rule lands after January 18 and the effective date is January 18, 2027.

sections.part: 1 · The GENIUS Act and its clocks

rows.title: who-may-issue
fields: Only a 'permitted payment stablecoin issuer' may issue a payment stablecoin in the United States. That means a U.S.-formed company that is (A) an approved subsidiary of an insured bank, (B) a federal qualified issuer (a nonbank or uninsured national bank approved by the OCC), or (C) a state qualified issuer.
It shall be unlawful for any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States. (Sec. 3(a))

sources.label: GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27

rows.title: definition
fields: A digital asset used or designed for payment or settlement whose issuer is obligated to convert, redeem or repurchase it for a fixed amount of money and promises (or creates a reasonable expectation of) a stable value. National currencies, bank deposits and securities are excluded.
does not include a digital asset that— (i) is a national currency; (ii) is a deposit ...; (iii) is a security ... (Sec. 2(22)(B))

sources.label: GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27

rows.title: reserves
fields: At least 1:1 reserves limited to: U.S. coins and currency; demand deposits; Treasury bills, notes or bonds with 93 days or less to maturity; money received under repurchase agreements backed by such Treasury bills; overnight reverse repurchase agreements collateralized by Treasuries; shares of registered government money market funds investing in these; other similarly liquid federal government assets the regulator approves; and tokenized forms of these. Reserves may not be pledged, rehypothecated or reused except in narrow cases. The issuer must publish its reserve composition monthly, and the month-end report must be examined by a registered public accounting firm.
Reserves required under paragraph (1)(A) may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused (Sec. 4(a)(2))

Clause (vi) is summarized from the quoted fragment 'securities issued by an investment company registered under section 8(a) of the Investment Company Act of 1940'; the full limits on which funds qualify were not re-read in this pass.

sources.label: GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27

rows.title: interest-ban
fields: Neither a permitted issuer nor a foreign issuer may pay a holder any form of interest or yield, in cash, tokens or anything else, solely for holding, using or keeping the coin. The ban names issuers; it does not name exchanges or other distributors. The OCC's March 2, 2026 proposed rule (not final) would presume the issuer is paying holders when it has an arrangement with an affiliate or related third party that pays them (proposed 12 CFR 15.10(c)(4), 91 FR 10202).

No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. (Sec. 4(a)(11))
Whether the OCC presumption is rebuttable, and exactly how 'related third party' is defined, were not fully read; the CLARITY market-structure bill's reward limits have not become law.

sources.label: GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27
OCC proposed GENIUS rule (91 FR 10202), proposed 12 CFR 15.10(c)(4)

rows.title: lawful-orders
fields: A 'lawful order' is one that requires a person to seize, freeze, burn or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins it issued. A permitted issuer may issue only if it has the technical ability to comply with such orders. A foreign issuer's coin may be offered in the U.S. only if the issuer can and will comply with lawful orders.
requires a person to seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person (Sec. 2(16)(A))

sources.label: GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27

rows.title: platform-cutoff-and-size
fields: Starting three years after enactment (July 18, 2028), a digital-asset service provider may not offer or sell a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States unless a permitted issuer issued it (foreign issuers have a separate route). A state qualified issuer that passes the $10 billion outstanding threshold must move to the federal framework within 360 days unless its regulator grants a waiver.

beginning on the date that is 3 years after the date of enactment of this Act, it shall be unlawful for a digital asset service provider to offer or sell a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States, unless the payment stablecoin is issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer (Sec. 3(b)(1), assembled from quoted fragments)

The $10 billion figure is from the library's July 2026 cards; the fetched text of Sec. 4(d) referred to 'such threshold' without the number being quoted back. The foreign-issuer comparability provision is cited by the library as 12 U.S.C. 5916; its section number in the Act was not confirmed here. The Act's general effective date is kept in the genius_act_milestones master (January 18, 2027).

fields: If books disagree, which record decides the holder, balance, or obligation?

Issuer registers, transfer-agent files, depository entitlement books, bank accounts, and networks can each describe a different legal relationship. Identify the controlling record for this issue and event.
Issuer; recordkeeping transfer agent; depository; bank; network operator.

CCP; clearing member; settlement bank; liquidity provider; collateral manager.

fields: What asset moves, in which accounts, and when is each obligation final?

Securities delivery, cash posting, token transfer, payout, and redemption can have different finality points. Name whether the event is technical confirmation, book-entry posting, contractual discharge, or statutory finality.
Settlement operator; depository; bank; cash issuer; participant.
Settlement rule; cash-asset identity; account-entry timing; finality and insolvency clause.
A two-leg settlement receipt with named assets, timestamps, and finality rules.

Completion creates customer, participant, depository, transfer-agent, issuer, and sometimes network postings. Servicing covers distributions, votes, corporate actions, maturity, redemption, and reporting.
Posting records; reconciliation schedule; servicing agreement; exception reports.

fields: Asset classification uses the Commission's definitions of functional and decentralized, while fulfillment of essential-managerial-effort promises uses the functionality or decentralization threshold the issuer itself represented. A pure receipt evidences the depositor's continuing ownership of a stated deposited asset without changing its rights or adding separate economics. Still open: Separate ordinary post-functional service from unfulfilled issuer promises, new profit-linked undertakings and the actual administration of holder rights.

Successor assumption preserves the promise relationship; by contrast, issuer statements likely do not create a new investment contract once a functional system has no central party capable of controlling success or failure. Still open: Prove the succession instrument, remaining obligations, control distribution, abandonment or completion facts and any later promise rather than treating a handoff or decentralization slogan as dispositive.
Corporation Finance staff guidance issued September 25, 2026; nonbinding and not Commission action.

Nine staff answers apply the March Commission interpretation to two functionality clocks, staking receipts, pure-receipt ownership and no-rehypothecation conditions, utility marketing, successor promises, post-functional development, central-party absence, buybacks and secondary-platform promoter status.

The FAQs refine legal analysis but create no rule, registration, exemption, safe harbor, venue permission, asset approval or operating receipt. The March interpretation remains the Commission-level object, and Regulation Crypto Assets remains proposed.

fields: Custody scope depends on the crypto asset's legal classification and account type; self-custody would also require a written Article 8 financial-asset and securities-intermediary election. Possession of any portion of key materials can establish custody; only designated supervised persons may hold keys and at least two people, including management, must jointly authorize movement. Per-client address segregation, State trust financial statements, internal control reports, network reconciliation and related-cash limits would create a custody protection layer. The proposal recognizes network records and custody controls but does not propose a general exception for assets held on non-custodian trading platforms and does not create a universal DeFi route. Still open: Prove venue authority, cash leg, delivery-versus-payment, technical confirmation, legal discharge, staking or protocol control and finality for each leg.

Addresses, balances, transactions, client statements or electronic views, Article 8 agreements, annual reviews, board records and independent reports would form a joined but multi-record custody constitution. Commission proposal issued October 1, 2026; not final, effective, compliant or operating.

The 760-page proposal would create asset-specific adviser self-custody only while no qualified custodian will maintain the covered asset, add a conditional State trust company route, apply fund-board oversight, treat key possession as custody, require segregation, joint authorization, cybersecurity, independent control reporting and Article 8 treatment, and permit qualifying onchain regulatory records with examiner-readable offchain completion.

The proposal grants no present permission, does not cover every crypto asset or account, supplies no general exchange-custody or DeFi exception, does not make a chain the universal ownership record and does not prove a named adviser, fund, custodian, asset, wallet, protocol or transaction complies or operates.

fields: Network-token and ancillary-asset provisions would create new federal classification and disclosure branches for some digital-asset transactions. Still open: Enactment, implementing rules and product-specific facts remain necessary; the draft does not classify every existing Hub asset.

Spot exchanges, brokers, dealers, custodians and persons controlling covered DeFi functions would receive proposed registration or compliance routes after the required rules. Still open: EHF26724 is not law, its amendment fields remain blank, and no Hub actor receives a current registration, exemption or charter power from it.

Customer-property, segregation, custody, disclosure and books-and-records provisions would add qualification requirements by intermediary function. Still open: The draft does not make a blockchain the authoritative legal record for every asset or replace issue-specific contracts and record hierarchies.

Revised developer protections would expressly cover specified non-controlling development, validation, node, oracle, bandwidth and user-controlled wallet activities for named money-transmission categories. Still open: The shield is proposed and function-specific, removes the earlier express 18 U.S.C. 1960 reference, and does not create a derivatives or general-conduct immunity.

Stablecoin rewards would carry a contingent Treasury deposit-flight circuit breaker, while federal and insured credit unions would gain express parity for otherwise-authorized DLT and digital-asset activity. Registration, customer-property, disclosure and reporting provisions would add function-specific recordkeeping and servicing duties. Still open: Issuer, transfer-agent, custodian, exchange, broker, bank and network records remain separate and would require implementing rules and contracts.

The draft adds affiliate-conflict controls, exchange proprietary-trading limits, preserved state consumer-protection routes and a permanent ethics enforcement regime with specified federal and state remedies. Still open: These are proposed duties, not present findings that a named Hub company or official complied, violated, caused harm or bears a particular loss.
Sponsors' final draft released September 14, 2026; not filed substitute text or operative law.

The 635-page draft retains four divisions and would create coordinated SEC, Treasury, banking-agency and CFTC routes for digital assets, spot intermediaries and controlled DeFi. It adds affiliate-conflict and proprietary-trading controls, a stablecoin deposit-flight circuit breaker, credit-union parity, revised developer protections and a permanent digital-asset ethics regime.
This case changes future qualification questions only. It grants no present permission, classification, registration or compliance status to any Hub actor, asset, protocol or transaction.

rows.title: Tokenized NMS Stock Innovation Exemption
fields: The pool must contain Tokenized NMS Stock carrying the same company interest, voting, dividend and residual rights as the underlying NMS stock. Still open: An actual issue, tokenizer, holder-rights instrument and Securities Act route must still be identified. Synthetic exposures, rights and warrants are outside the defined stock category.

The order separates the TSV operator, affiliates, tokenizers, liquidity providers, participants, registered activities and service providers and requires public conflict disclosure. Still open: No Hub company or ecosystem is named as a TSV, Covered Firm, tokenizer, participant or service provider. Each legal entity and role must be proved from the eventual notice and contracts.

The Commission order is effective and supplies two temporary conditional exemptions through September 17, 2031. Still open: No venue may operate until its complete public notice has run for at least 30 calendar days. Existing broker-dealer and other participant obligations are not broadly waived.

Token holders must receive equivalent stock rights and the TSV must disclose the tokenization, legal and technical evaluation, wallets, chain, contracts, keys and correction-related controls. Still open: The order does not make the AMM, wallet or chain the issuer's authoritative ownership record or grant transfer-agent relief. The actual record hierarchy remains issue-specific.

Participant access is permissioned even though the application must be public and deployed on public, permissionless DLT. The TSV sets admission standards, pool parameters and administrative controls. Still open: The first notice must identify identity checks, differentiated treatment, upgrade, pause, override, privacy, MEV and service-provider controls. Public infrastructure does not mean public market access.
Step: Clear the obligation and assemble resources

A Covered Firm may provide own-account Tokenized NMS Stock liquidity and disclose agreements, fees, rebates and token incentives. The TSV itself may not finance purchases or lend, borrow or hypothecate assets on the venue. Still open: The order supplies no CCP, custody, external financing, haircut, default waterfall or token-inventory receipt. Persistent net XRP or other token inventory remains unproved.
Step: Settle each leg and name finality

The order permits a venue architecture capable of self-custody, extended hours and faster settlement and requires disclosure of actual clearing and settlement arrangements. Still open: Near-instant settlement is a possible benefit, not a required or proven legal-finality result. Each securities, crypto, money-market-fund and cash leg needs its own finality and insolvency analysis.

The TSV must retain detailed interest, execution, permissioning, wallet, fee, halt, ADV, notice and event records; equivalent voting, dividend and issuer-communication rights must continue. Still open: Trade reporting within ten minutes is not the same as SIP reporting or proof that issuer, transfer-agent, custodian and participant books reconciled. Corporate-action servicing remains product-specific.
Step: Repair, allocate loss and prove the result

Underlying-market halts must carry across; significant operational events require participant and SEC notice and remediation; records remain examinable by the Commission. Still open: The order can require disclosure that surveillance, complaint or other protections are absent. It does not itself provide a complete customer-loss, clearing-default, custody-failure or smart-contract remedy.
Effective SEC exemptive order through September 17, 2031; no operating TSV established at the saved cutoff.

Release 34-106402 conditionally exempts a Tokenized Securities Venue from the Exchange Act definition of exchange and a qualifying own-account AMM liquidity provider from the dealer definition. Permissioned pools must use auditable public applications deployed on public, permissionless DLT; at least one leg must be Tokenized NMS Stock, and the other may be another such stock, any non-security crypto asset or a tokenized money market fund.

The order opens a venue category, not a named venue, chain, token or product. A complete TSV notice must run for at least 30 calendar days, and issuer, issuance, record, custody, clearing, settlement, participant and failure rules remain separate.

rows.title: BUIDL · subscribe and record fund shares
fields: Follow the fund share, subscription money and official register. This maps contractual responsibilities; individual payment receipts remain unresolved.

Title: Eligible offering access · Lanes: Asset: Text: BUIDL is offered through the named placement and access function for eligible investors.; Boundary: Product-specific eligibility and offering restrictions remain controlling; placement authority is not transfer-agent authority.; Status: documented; Money: Text: The payment instruction, bank, funding account, and receipt for a particular subscription are not mapped.; Boundary: The saved BUIDL records do not establish a subscription-payment route or completed cash posting.; Status: unresolved; Record: Text: Eligibility to enter an offering is documented separately from the shareholder record.; Boundary: Admission does not by itself establish a recorded fund-share entitlement.; Status: documented

Title: Fund-share issuance and control book · Lanes: Asset: Text: The fund issuer creates shares; Securitize acts under its appointment.; Boundary: Manager, fund, and transfer agent are separate persons and systems.; Status: documented; Money: Text: Issuance requires confirmation of receipt or credit of subscription funds to the custodian.; Boundary: Contractual condition in section 2.3; a particular investor’s payment receipt is not provided.; Status: documented; Record: Text: Securitize maintains the issuer’s share register.; Boundary: The control book is distinct from a wallet, bridge, or chain consensus record.; Status: documented

Title: Named network representation · Lanes: Asset: Text: BUIDL has named live representations on supported networks, including Ethereum.; Boundary: Network availability is not proof that a network is the exclusive or legally authoritative register.; Status: documented; Money: Text: No network representation establishes a subscription payment or cash settlement path.; Boundary: The saved evidence does not link the representation to a particular money movement.; Status: unresolved; Record: Text: Securitize's multichain model uses Wormhole infrastructure while the regulated control book remains external to transport.; Boundary: Transport does not replace the transfer-agent record or determine legal title.; Status: documented

Title: Servicing and correction · Lanes: Asset: Text: Ongoing BUIDL share servicing remains governed by the reviewed transfer-agent agreement.; Boundary: The terms and required instructions determine whether a transfer is recognized.; Status: documented; Money: Text: Cash redemption route and payout completion for this case are not documented here.; Boundary: The case does not treat a separate RLUSD exchange option as a subscription or fiat-payout proof.; Status: unresolved; Record: Text: Securitize may refuse a transfer lacking valid authority.; Boundary: Contract sections 3.2–3.5 address transfer instructions and adverse claims; network consensus is not that authorization.; Status: documented

rows.title: USDC · issue, transfer and redeem
fields: Follow the token, reserve money and issuer records. Direct redemption depends on customer eligibility; token movement does not prove bank payout.

Title: Mint access and eligibility · Lanes: Asset: Text: Circle Mint provides the access path for an eligible institution to seek issuance of USDC.; Boundary: KYC and service access are mapped; a particular bank-funding instruction and posting receipt are absent.; Status: documented; Money: Text: A specific incoming USD payment route or settlement receipt is not mapped.; Boundary: Access eligibility does not prove bank funding, reserve receipt, or final settlement of a given order.; Status: unresolved; Record: Text: The applicable legal issuer is the issuer-side liability and instruction authority for USDC.; Boundary: The issuer perimeter remains distinct from Circle Mint access and from every supported network.; Status: documented

Title: Reserve and native mint · Lanes: Asset: Text: Native USDC is minted under issuer instruction on a selected supported chain.; Boundary: This generic trace does not specify the selected-chain execution for a particular issuance.; Status: documented; Money: Text: Dollar assets enter an issuer-specific segregated reserve pool.; Boundary: The reserve-pool role is mapped, not a transaction-level reserve inflow posting.; Status: documented; Record: Text: The issuer's USDC obligation and reserve records remain separate from token state.; Boundary: Chain state does not itself establish the issuer liability or reserve position.; Status: documented

Title: Token transport · Lanes: Asset: Text: USDC can move through wallets and supported transport mechanisms.; Boundary: The mechanisms are alternatives, not successive mandatory hops in one transaction.; Status: documented; Money: Text: No token transfer alone establishes an FX conversion, bank payout, or new fiat settlement.; Boundary: Token transport is not evidence of completed money movement outside the issuer claim.; Status: unresolved; Record: Text: Technical token state and transport are distinct from the issuer liability record and redemption eligibility.; Boundary: Chain finality does not guarantee direct Circle redemption eligibility.; Status: documented

Title: Redemption and bank payout · Lanes: Asset: Text: USDC is burned under applicable issuer eligibility rules when redeemed.; Boundary: No transaction-specific burn receipt is supplied.; Status: documented; Money: Text: Reserve liquidity is intended to become bank USD payout, but a separate direct-Circle payout completion card is not mapped.; Boundary: Do not use a distinct Tazapay conversion/local-payout route to fill this direct-redemption gap.; Status: unresolved; Record: Text: Issuer redemption terms govern the obligation; token burn and bank payout remain distinct evidence points.; Boundary: Burn does not by itself prove completed bank payout or discharge for a specific customer.; Status: documented

sections.part: 4 · The SEC's crypto custody proposal (S7-2026-35)

rows.title: Ordinary advisory-account crypto scope
fields: For an ordinary advisory client, the custody rule reaches a crypto asset only when it is a fund or security.
Crypto form alone does not create the custody perimeter; asset classification and account type remain prior gates.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Regulated-fund crypto scope
fields: For regulated-fund accounts, the adviser and Investment Company Act routes extend to crypto assets that are securities or similar investments.
Fund and ordinary advisory-account perimeters are related but not identical.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: No-qualified-custodian gate
fields: Self-custody is available only when, after written due inquiry, no qualified custodian will maintain the particular covered asset; cost cannot support the determination.
Self-custody is a residual market-failure lane, not a general preference or best-interest option.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Quarterly custodian-market re-test
fields: The no-qualified-custodian determination is reassessed at least quarterly.
Route eligibility is a recurring market clock rather than a one-time permission.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Migration when custody becomes available
fields: When a qualified custodian becomes available, the adviser must transfer the asset as soon as reasonably practicable.
The custody route can expire asset by asset and force an operational migration.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Any key-material portion can establish custody
fields: Actual possession of any portion of necessary key materials can constitute adviser self-custody, including a share in a multisignature or MPC design.
Custody turns on practical key participation, not the wallet product label.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Designated supervised key holders
fields: Only adviser-designated supervised persons may possess key materials; a fund board designates the persons for a regulated fund.
The wallet becomes a named human and governance perimeter.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Two-person joint authorization
fields: Movement requires joint authorization by at least two designated people, including a management person and, for a fund, a fund officer.
The proposal rejects single-person institutional control and makes management participation inspectable.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Technology-provider control boundary
fields: A third-party technology provider may support the custody system only if it cannot access key materials or unilaterally move the assets; the adviser remains responsible.
Vendor capability and legal custody are separated by actual access and movement power.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Single-employee adviser cannot use route
fields: The two-person and management requirements make the proposed self-custody route unavailable to a single-employee adviser.
Institutional form and staffing become eligibility conditions.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Per-client address segregation
fields: Each client's self-custodied assets must be held in one or more addresses containing only that client's crypto assets; adviser omnibus addresses are not permitted.
Segregation is made visible at the address layer, with direct privacy, fee, recovery and operational consequences.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Cyber assessment, response and recovery
fields: Written crypto-custody cybersecurity assessment is required before custody, at least annually and after material change, with prevention, detection, mitigation, remediation, response and recovery controls.
Cybersecurity becomes part of the custody constitution rather than a detached technology policy.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Independent operating-effectiveness report
fields: An independent public accountant must issue an internal control report within six months after self-custody begins and at least annually thereafter.
Institutional custody needs recurring third-party evidence, not a one-time technology certification.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: SOC 1 Type 2 operating-evidence threshold
fields: A SOC 1 Type 2 report may qualify because it tests operating effectiveness over time; a Type 1 report does not.
Design assertions are distinguished from evidence that controls actually operated.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Books-to-network reconciliation
fields: The internal control report must cover reconciliation of the adviser's records to the crypto network.
Network state and institutional books become separate records that must be joined rather than presumed identical.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Qualifying onchain regulatory records
fields: Crypto-related required records may be maintained onchain only when true, accurate, current, retained for the full period and promptly producible in human-readable, reasonably usable form.
A chain can host the compliance record without becoming the universal ownership, accounting or remedy record.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Offchain completion of network records
fields: Offchain records must supplement the network when ownership, client identity, contact information, authorization, metadata or another required field is absent.
Public address data is expressly incomplete as a customer and legal ledger.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Quarterly client statement or transmission
fields: At least quarterly the adviser must provide a statement or qualifying human-readable transmission showing address, network, balances and transactions, with an instruction to compare against the network.
Client-facing evidence is a distinct record layer and privacy networks may require a supplemental view.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Full position and transaction reconstruction
fields: Adviser records must reconstruct positions and transactions by client, account, address, amount, destination, authorization and relevant metadata, including specified DeFi and staking information.
The transaction constitution includes accepted instruction and beneficial ownership, not only the onchain event.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Mandatory Article 8 election
fields: The adviser and client must agree in writing that each self-custodied asset is a financial asset and that the adviser acts as securities intermediary under applicable State law.
Key possession is translated into an entitlement and priority frame rather than treated as direct investor possession by default.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: No federal insurance created
fields: The Article 8 election is intended to improve property and creditor-priority treatment but creates no FDIC or SIPC protection.
Property characterization, insurance and actual recovery remain separate claims.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: No standalone Commission loss report
fields: The proposed text does not require a standalone adviser loss report to the Commission, although the release requests comment on one.
Board notice, control exceptions and public reporting do not yet form a complete regulator incident feed.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Regulated-fund board overlay
fields: A fund board reviews the no-qualified-custodian determination before custody and quarterly, and makes a reasonable-care determination initially and annually, with notice of serious events and adverse control opinions.
Fund custody adds a formal governance and escalation record above adviser operations.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Conditional State trust custodian class
fields: A State-law trust company supervised and examined by a State banking authority and authorized for fiduciary powers may qualify for covered crypto custody after route-specific due inquiry.
Charter status opens a possible route but does not establish company-, asset-, contract- or date-specific qualification.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Annual State trust due inquiry
fields: Before use and annually, the adviser or fund must document authorization, safeguarding policies, U.S. GAAP audited financials, a current internal control report and segregation.
The route depends on recurring evidence rather than the trust charter alone.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Crypto-only State trust route
fields: State trust qualified-custodian status is limited to covered crypto assets and related cash or cash equivalents unless the company separately qualifies as a bank.
A crypto trust route is not a general custody or banking permission.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Capital, insurance and loss floors unresolved
fields: Federal capital, insurance, liquidity, indemnity, rehypothecation, loss-allocation and minimum recovery floors are principally questions for comment, not proposed conditions.
The protection stack cannot be inferred from the words State trust company.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: No general DeFi custody pathway
fields: The proposal asks about staking, receipt tokens, protocol control, bugs, insurance, collateral and recourse but creates no special DeFi custody exception.
Protocol capability does not supply a permitted custody route.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: No trading-platform custody exception
fields: The proposal asks about a possible limited platform route, including a 24-hour construct, but proposes no general non-custodian trading-platform exception.
The SEC's onchain execution adapter remains legally separate from custody.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Rule 17f-1 broker-dealer custody substitution
fields: Regulated funds and BDCs may use any registered broker-dealer whose custody is subject to rule 15c3-3 or a Commission-determined equivalent, replacing enumerated legacy conditions.
The control model changes from a list of custody mechanics to reliance on a broader customer-protection regime.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: PCAOB registration and inspection proxy removed
fields: Certain custody audits, surprise examinations and control reports would retain independent-public-accountant and professional-standard requirements while dropping the PCAOB registration and inspection condition.
Accountant independence and work standards survive, but the institutional qualification proxy changes.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Form ADV self-custody measurement surface
fields: Form ADV would report custody basis, approximate value, client count, address count, accountant, opinion, statement method and pooled-vehicle use; Item 9.F does not list every wallet-address string.
Form ADV Item 9 and Schedule D 9.C
If adopted and filed, the form could produce recurring evidence of route use, scale and assurance providers.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Network-name and tokenized-fund reporting
fields: Schedule D and Form N-CEN would identify tokenized funds, applicable crypto networks, State trust use and self-custody use.
Form N-CEN; Schedule D 7.B.(1) Q25(h), Q29
The forms could become a public measurement layer for regulated network adoption, but reporting is not approval or operation proof.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Self-custody control-report cost
fields: The SEC estimates a $376,000 annual independent internal-control report per affected self-custody adviser within a $433.833 million annual adviser self-custody cost estimate.
Compliance economics may concentrate institutional self-custody among scaled advisers, accountants and control vendors.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: Estimated route populations
fields: The analysis assumes 823 adviser self-custody users, 715 fund self-custody users, 1,645 adviser State trust users and 1,430 fund State trust users; these are assumptions, not observed adoption.
Future final estimates and real filings can be compared against a fixed baseline without treating assumptions as market share.

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal

rows.title: SEC LLM-assisted adviser census
fields: The SEC used an LLM followed by manual review to identify advisers providing or planning crypto-related services; question 340 asks whether the method is appropriate.
The release supplies a government-AI evidence-method case linking model classification to an economically significant rulemaking baseline.

sections.part: 4 · The SEC's crypto custody proposal (S7-2026-35)

rows.title: Question 1
fields: Pursuant to the proposed adviser self-custody rule, an adviser would be permitted to have self-custody of a client’s crypto asset without maintaining it at a qualified custodian, provided that the adviser complies with the requirements of the proposed adviser self-custody rule. Should an adviser be permitted to have self-custody of client crypto assets, including crypto assets of a regulated fund, as proposed? Why or why not?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 2
fields: Do commenters agree that qualified custodian availability is a particularly acute problem for certain kinds of crypto assets, such as nascent or novel crypto assets? If so, what types of crypto assets raise heightened challenges to finding available qualified custodians to maintain them? To what extent would the proposed rule permitting crypto asset custody at State trust companies discussed below (see section II.C) alleviate these challenges?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 3
fields: The Advisers Act custody rule excepts securities that meet the description of privately offered securities from the qualified custodian requirement on the basis that they are hard to steal. 124 Privately offered securities are securities that are: (i) acquired from the issuer in a transaction or chain of transactions not involving any public offering; (ii) uncertificated, and ownership thereof is recorded only on the books of the issuer or its transfer agent in the name of the client; and (iii) transferable only with prior consent of the issuer or holders of the outstanding securities of the issuer. Crypto assets would not be able to meet this exception if, for example, records of their ownership are not recorded only on the books of the issuer or its transfer agent in the name of the client, or if they can be transferred without the prior consent of the issuer. Are there crypto assets that could qualify as privately offered securities? If so, what characteristics of such crypto assets and/or their crypto networks satisfy the conditions of the privately offered securities exception? If there are crypto assets that could qualify as privately offered securities, should the privately offered securities exception be amended to except the adviser from the conditions of the proposed adviser self-custody rule with respect to any such crypto assets in the adviser’s self- custody? Why or why not? If yes, how should the privately offered securities exception be amended, if at all, to accommodate characteristics unique to securities that are crypto assets and what conditions should apply to such crypto assets under the exception to ensure that the privately offered securities exception continues to exempt only those crypto assets that have features similar to privately offered securities that provide external safeguards against the kinds of abuse the custody rule seeks to prevent?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 4
fields: Is our understanding correct that some advisers engage in extensive due diligence of a crypto asset beginning in its early stage development, and that such advisers may acquire expertise on the functioning and operation of the associated crypto network, potentially allowing them to be well-positioned to securely self-custody the crypto asset? If not, why not? How does the adviser’s due diligence of the crypto asset position the adviser to be better situated than a traditional custodian to custody the crypto asset? Does the adviser’s involvement via the due diligence of the crypto asset create or enhance any conflicts of interest that the proposed custody rule amendments should uniquely address?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 5
fields: In a Commission interpretation addressing the application of certain Federal securities laws to certain types of crypto assets and certain transactions involving crypto assets, the Commission stated that non-security crypto assets may be offered and sold subject to an investment contract, which is a security.125 Is any guidance or additional changes to the Commission’s custody rules needed to address non-security crypto assets that are subject to an investment contract?

rows.title: Question 6
fields: Would the proposed safeguards under the adviser self-custody rule raise any particular challenges for smaller advisers or regulated funds with smaller advisers? If so, what could we do to help mitigate those challenges?

rows.title: Question 7
fields: Are there any services or business practices engaged in by advisers that could cause an adviser to become subject to regulation or become regulated entities under other regulatory frameworks outside of the Commission’s rules (for example, regulations governing banks and money transmitters) if advisers were permitted to hold crypto assets in self-custody pursuant to the adviser self-custody rule?

rows.title: Question 8
fields: Are the terms and definitions proposed in connection with the proposed adviser self- custody rule (“crypto network,” “crypto asset,” “crypto asset address,” “key materials,” “self-custody” and “distributed crypto asset”) clear? Why or why not? Do they accurately reflect the current technology for crypto assets and are they flexible enough to accommodate technological developments in the future? Are there other definitions of these terms we should use? For example, given how fundamental the term “crypto asset” is to this proposal, is there a more specific definition we should consider? Is the definition too limiting or too encompassing? Does the definition for “crypto asset” scope in the appropriate range of assets as applied to registered advisers and regulated funds? Is the term “self-custody,” as used in this proposal, appropriate to describe an adviser holding a client’s crypto asset, or a regulated fund holding through an adviser a crypto asset, without maintaining it with a permitted custodian? Instead of “self-custody,” is there a more apt term to describe such custodial arrangements for crypto assets?

rows.title: Question 9
fields: Are there any defined terms that we either should not adopt or that we should change in the final rule?

rows.title: Question 10
fields: Are there additional terms used in the proposed adviser self-custody rule that we should define?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 11
fields: As noted above, the proposed Advisers Act custody rule would continue to apply to client assets that are funds or securities (and would be amended to apply to securities and similar investments held for the accounts of regulated funds that are subject to the proposed adviser self-custody rule), and we express our view that tokenized deposits and payment stablecoins issued by stablecoin issuers that are permitted payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act and foreign payment stablecoin issuers registered pursuant to section 18 of the GENIUS Act are crypto assets that are digital representations of funds subject to the Advisers Act custody rule. Are there other types of crypto assets, if any, that need clarification as to whether they are digital representations of “funds” subject to the Advisers Act custody rule, and why?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 12
fields: As noted above, “crypto asset” for purposes of this proposal would include digital securities, commonly known as “tokenized” securities. There are a variety of models used to tokenize securities, which may vary in terms of structure and the rights afforded to holders.146 What guidance or adjustments to the Commission’s custody rules, if any, are needed to address the custody of tokenized securities? Are there any circumstances in which maintaining the associated crypto asset at a permitted custodian, or in self-custody by an adviser pursuant to the proposed adviser self- custody rule, would not be sufficient to effectively hold the tokenized security in custody under the Commission’s custody rules?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 13
fields: Is the proposed definition for self-custody appropriate in imputing self-custody to an adviser that possesses any portion (including a non-controlling share) of the key materials associated with its client’s crypto asset? If not, what portion of a crypto asset’s key materials in an adviser’s possession should confer self-custody on the adviser and trigger the application of the self-custody requirements to the adviser? For example, should self-custody be conferred on an adviser only when the adviser holds all or a controlling share of the key materials? How should a “controlling” private key share be defined for this purpose? If the custody rule did not confer self- custody on an adviser that holds a non-controlling portion of the key materials, what protections, if any, should instead apply to ensure that the key materials held with the adviser are appropriately safeguarded and how, if at all, should such protections differ from the conditions in the proposed adviser self-custody rule?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 14
fields: Currently, under what circumstances, if any, is the private key to a client’s crypto asset shared among the adviser and third parties? Which parties in those circumstances would hold the shares of a private key, and for what purpose? For example, do wallet solution providers ever need to retain a portion of the user’s key materials? Is doing so necessary to enhance the security of key materials?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 15
fields: Under this proposal, a qualified custodian maintaining a client’s crypto asset would not be able to share the key materials to the crypto asset with an adviser because, if the adviser held any portion of the key materials, the adviser would be required to comply with the self-custody requirements, which are limited to circumstances where no qualified custodian is available. Are there circumstances today in which a qualified custodian (e.g., a bank) would maintain a client’s crypto asset and some portion of its key materials while the adviser retains a non-controlling portion of the key materials, such that the adviser does not have the unilateral ability to access and/or move the crypto asset? If so, what would be the purpose of these arrangements? Are custodial risks, such as the risk of misappropriation by the adviser or the loss of the crypto asset resulting from the loss of any private key held with the adviser, mitigated in these arrangements, so that only some of the proposed adviser self-custody rule’s requirements (or none at all) should apply to the adviser? If yes, which of the proposed adviser self-custody rule’s requirements should apply to the adviser in these arrangements? In such arrangements, should the adviser self-custody rule apply only to the portion of the key materials held with the adviser, and should other applicable requirements under the Advisers Act custody rule (e.g., the qualified custodian requirement, the notice requirement, and the account statement delivery requirement) apply to the portion of the key materials held with a qualified custodian? Would it be possible, in practice, to apply the Advisers Act custody rule to different shares of key materials distributed between a qualified custodian and an adviser?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 16
fields: Alternatively, are there circumstances in which a qualified custodian would share the key materials to a client’s crypto asset with the adviser, such that neither the adviser nor the qualified custodian would have exclusive control over the crypto asset? If so, what would be the purpose of these arrangements? If yes, would the qualified custodian and the adviser share control over the crypto asset, or would each independently have control over the crypto asset, in that each party independently would have the unilateral ability to access and move the crypto asset? Is the loss of the crypto asset resulting from the loss of any private key share mitigated or increased in these arrangements where neither the adviser nor the qualified custodian has exclusive control over the crypto asset?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 17
fields: Under this proposal, the proposed related person QC rule, as opposed to the adviser self-custody rule, would apply to custodial arrangements where the adviser, or its related person, holds all of the key materials to a client’s crypto asset, in each case in its capacity as a qualified custodian. Should the proposed adviser self-custody rule apply instead of the related person QC rule to these arrangements? Why or why not? Would the proposed related person QC rule and the internal control report requirement thereunder, as proposed, sufficiently address risks of adviser fraud and misappropriation through the adviser and its related persons that are qualified custodians maintaining client crypto assets?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 18
fields: Are there circumstances today in which an adviser’s related person that is a qualified custodian would share a client crypto asset’s key materials with a qualified custodian that is not the related person of an adviser? How should the requirements of the related person QC rule apply to those arrangements?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 19
fields: The Advisers Act custody rule sets forth conditions that must be met in order to overcome the presumption that a related person of the adviser is not operationally independent of the adviser.163 Are there circumstances today in which an adviser’s use of a related person that is operationally independent of the adviser would raise issues related to the proposed adviser self-custody rule? For example, do advisers today utilize related persons that are operationally independent of the adviser to hold client crypto assets outside of a traditional custodian, and if so, what functions do such related persons serve for purposes of self-custody, and how do advisers oversee the practices of such related persons in light of their operational independence from the adviser?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 20
fields: In what circumstances, if any, would multiple qualified custodians need to hold copies of the key materials to a crypto asset or share portions of the key materials to a crypto asset? Should the Advisers Act custody rule prohibit the sharing of access to a client crypto asset’s key materials by multiple qualified custodians? Why or why not?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 21
fields: Is our view provided under section II.A.1c)(1) (“Use of Service Providers”) regarding the use of service providers and related persons sufficiently clear? Should we provide any additional clarification regarding an adviser’s use of service providers and related persons for purposes of the proposed adviser self-custody rule? If so, what clarifications are needed? What, if any, additional protections are needed in self- custody arrangements for crypto assets that involve the use of service providers and related persons? What arrangements involving the use of service providers and/or related persons for purposes of crypto asset custody that are commonly in place today would be prohibited by limiting access to crypto asset key materials to qualified custodians and registered investment advisers complying with the adviser self- custody rule?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 22
fields: Are there any instances today where a service provider (including a related person that is not a registered adviser) could have possession and control of a crypto asset even without access to the key materials to such crypto asset? If so, for what services are those providers used, and what protections are in place to prevent such service providers from unilaterally and impermissibly moving a crypto asset for unauthorized purposes?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 23
fields: In what circumstances, if any, does a service provider have access to a portion, but not all, of a crypto asset’s key materials? Do service providers in those instances have possession and control of the crypto asset, or otherwise the ability to unilaterally move a crypto asset? Notwithstanding whether a service provider in those instances has the unilateral ability to move a crypto asset, does a service provider having access to a portion of the key materials still raise custodial risks such as the risk of loss resulting from the loss of the key share? If not, should the adviser be permitted to engage such service provider, and if so, what protections should apply to those arrangements where a service provider has access to a portion of the key materials, to ensure that such access does not result in the loss or theft of the crypto asset?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 24
fields: Are commenters aware of any examples of advisers using related persons that are not qualified custodians to safeguard crypto assets including their key materials? If so, what type of entities are such related persons that provide custodial services for client crypto assets in an adviser’s custody? Are these examples necessary and helpful to investor protection? Why or why not?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 25
fields: Do advisers anticipate that they would enter into separate custodial agreements with clients for whom they hold crypto assets in self-custody, or would advisers specify the terms and conditions of self-custody services within the client’s overall investment advisory agreement? Whether reflected in a separate agreement with the client or otherwise, an adviser holding a client’s crypto asset in self-custody—and not any third party assisting the adviser in these efforts—would be responsible for the safekeeping of the crypto asset and compliance with the proposed adviser self- custody rule. Should the adviser be required to acknowledge and clearly delineate this responsibility in an agreement with the client?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 26
fields: Is our understanding correct that some third-party service providers offer key backup and recovery services? From a technical standpoint, what steps are involved in the key recovery process and which parties (e.g., the adviser, the client, the service provider) are required to be involved when the service provider recovers key materials? Could the key materials ever be recovered or reset in a way that would grant the service provider access to and control of the key materials, or deny the adviser exclusive access to and control over the key materials? If yes, under what circumstances could this occur? If not, what technology prevents this from happening? Could an adviser’s non-payment for the provider’s services ever result in the service provider gaining control of the adviser’s key materials or the service provider preventing the adviser from accessing the key materials? What technology prevents the service provider from doing this?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 27
fields: In what circumstances, if any, would an adviser have the authority to obtain possession of a client’s crypto asset’s key materials, but not actually possess the key materials? In what circumstances, if any, would an adviser have the authority to obtain possession of, but not actually possess, only a portion of the key materials to a client’s crypto asset? Is it more difficult for an adviser to misappropriate or lose a crypto asset when it has the authority to obtain possession of only a portion of a crypto asset’s key materials? Why or why not? If yes, should the custody rule’s protections apply to such crypto asset differently, and if so, how?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 28
fields: Are there any circumstances where an adviser would receive distributed crypto assets in connection with its advisory services but of a different kind from the crypto assets already in the adviser’s self-custody or maintained at a qualified custodian? How much advance notice, if any, would an adviser typically have of an upcoming airdrop? If the adviser receives an airdrop in connection with a crypto asset held in custody for a client, whether in the adviser’s self-custody or maintained at a qualified custodian, to what extent would the custodial infrastructure developed in connection with the client’s initial crypto asset be expected to apply to the airdropped crypto asset? To what extent would a qualified custodian be able to accommodate, or an adviser be able to adapt its self-custody infrastructure in order to hold, an airdropped crypto asset in full compliance with the Advisers Act custody rule upon receipt of the airdropped crypto asset?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 29
fields: Do advisers enter into written agreements with clients that include provisions relating to the custody treatment of distributed crypto assets? What do custodial agreements typically provide for with respect to the custody treatment of distributed crypto assets?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 30
fields: Should the airdrop provisions impose an outer limit of the time period within which an adviser and a regulated fund must come into full compliance with the Advisers Act and Investment Company Act custody rules, as applicable, with respect to an airdropped crypto asset, and if so, what should that time period be (e.g., no later than 30 business days, 60 days, or 90 days, after receipt of the airdrop), and why? In the case of airdropped crypto assets received for the account of a regulated fund, should the time period within which the regulated fund’s board must make the requisite determination pursuant to rule 17f-9 be more specific (for example, within 2 months of receiving the airdropped crypto asset or by the next regularly scheduled board meeting)?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 31
fields: When an adviser receives a distributed crypto asset in connection with its advisory services relating to crypto assets in its self-custody, how does the adviser ensure that the distributed crypto asset is correctly allocated to the relevant client? Does the adviser receive the distributed crypto asset in the wallet that holds the key materials to the crypto asset self-custodied for the corresponding client? Are there any circumstances where the distributed crypto asset is distributed into an adviser’s proprietary wallet, or the wallet of another client? Would the proposed segregation requirement under the adviser self-custody rule as discussed later in this proposal help ensure that distributed crypto assets are correctly allocated to the relevant parties? Are there any circumstances where an adviser treats a distributed crypto asset received in connection with its advisory services as belonging to the adviser, as opposed to the client, and if so, what are those circumstances? Should any amendments to the Advisers Act custody rule address the allocation of distributed crypto assets received in connection with the adviser’s custody of client crypto assets?

sources.label: SEC Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules; Crypto Custody Rules proposal (the home's own source)
SEC crypto-custody rulemaking page (the home's own source)

rows.title: Question 32
fields: Are there any limited exigent circumstances where an adviser or a regulated fund could unexpectedly receive a crypto asset, other than an airdropped crypto asset, in connection with the adviser’s advisory services provided to a client including a regulated fund? If so, what are those circumstances? fields: One temporary Commission order, two statutory-definition exemptions, twelve TSV condition modules, a separate Covered Firm lane, and thirty required public-notice fields.

Excluded: Synthetic exposure, Tokenized linked security, Tokenized security-based swap, Rights, Warrants, Primary issuance or initial offering on the TSV

sections.part: 7 · The Federal Reserve Board's GENIUS proposals (R-1899, R-1900)

rows.title: What the two Board proposals would set up
fields: The two Board proposals define a possible federal issuer operating constitution and an insured-state-member-bank application path. They regulate legal entities, claims, assets, controls, books and clocks; they do not approve a technology stack.

The GENIUS Stablecoin Rulebook page's reading of the two Federal Reserve Board proposals (the federal issuer operating rules and the insured-state-member-bank application path, docket R-1900), copied as written: 7 layers of gates (rule, effect, clock, watch), 9 clocks, a summary and the page's status word. Placed here because this file already holds the GENIUS Act's provisions (law_context) and the Board proposals implement that Act; crypto_rules.json excludes GENIUS rules by its home rule, and genius_act_milestones.json (the dated GENIUS home) was not among the files in this pass. The staged page data carried no source links, so this block is marked needs_primary_source until the Board's proposing releases are linked from genius_act_milestones.json.
Link the two Board proposing releases (docket R-1900) and their Federal Register dates from genius_act_milestones.json.
Decide whether this block moves to genius_act_milestones.json when that file is next edited.

rows.title: Authority and entry
fields: Rule: Identify the issuer, supervisor and approval route. An insured state member bank would apply through its Reserve Bank to the Board for a PPSI subsidiary, with proposed 30-day completeness and 120-day decision clocks. · Effect: Makes the legal entity, parent, control chain, consortium structure and proposed business plan visible before operation. · Clock: Proposed only; no operative R-1900 filing lane or actor-specific approval is established. · Watch: Federal Register publication, final rule, application materials, complete filing, decision and conditions.

Rule: Keep a payment stablecoin, deposit, security, native crypto asset and tokenized representation legally distinct. · Effect: Prevents a shared ledger or brand from collapsing the obligor, asset class, holder right and record authority into one object. · Clock: Definition remains proposed; statutory provisions retain their own effective state. · Watch: Final definitions, foreign-issuer treatment, deposit/securities boundary and named coin terms.
Which legal person may enter which supervisory lane?
Resolve issuer identity, control, parent and state/federal route before examining technology.

rows.title: Issuer business
fields: Rule: Issuance, redemption, reserve management/custody, stablecoin/key custody and related services form the core; lending and issuance as loan proceeds are prohibited, while material non-core activity generally needs permission. · Effect: Forces non-reserve assets, liabilities, affiliate businesses, gas holdings and service revenue into an explicit perimeter. · Clock: Proposed prudential boundary; no current business has been tested under the final calibration. · Watch: Final permitted-activity text and actor-specific written permissions.

Rule: Issuer-paid interest or yield for holding, using or retaining a stablecoin is prohibited; specified issuer-funded affiliate, service-provider and white-label paths face a rebuttable presumption. · Effect: Brings contracts, funding flows, branding and reward economics at distribution partners into the issuer perimeter. · Clock: Proposed related-party and rebuttal tests; not a final judgment on every independent reward program. · Watch: Final related-party definition, rebuttal evidence, distributor agreements and funding source.
What may the issuer do, hold, owe and outsource?
Separate core stablecoin functions from lending, material non-core assets/liabilities, affiliate economics and activities requiring permission.

rows.title: Backing and custody
fields: Rule: Maintain identifiable, segregated reserves at least equal to outstanding coins at fair value; tokenized forms of specified eligible categories must preserve identical legal rights. · Effect: Attaches eligibility to the underlying claim and rights rather than to a chain, token standard or vendor. · Clock: Proposed rule; daily 5 p.m. demonstration and any published eligibility list are not yet operative. · Watch: Final asset classes, liquidity/concentration limits, Board eligibility list and named tokenized-reserve opinion.

Rule: Covered assets require segregation, protection from creditor claims, possession/control, customer-level records and sub-custodian oversight; tokenized control turns on who can transfer without custodian consent. · Effect: Makes keys, wallet authority, omnibus subledgers and sub-custodian contracts part of the prudential control plane. · Clock: Proposed custody standard; self-custody remains outside where the provider lacks control and does not hold itself out as custodian. · Watch: Final control definition, qualified custodians, sub-custodian contracts and first examined custody stack.
What backs the claim, which rights travel through tokenization and who controls the assets?
Join 1:1 fair-value reserves, underlying-asset eligibility, identical rights, segregation, possession/control and sub-custodian records.

rows.title: Claim lifecycle
fields: Rule: Mint/burn authority, outstanding liability, reserve value, transaction processing, internal books and custodian records must remain reconcilable. · Effect: Treats on-chain supply as one record in a multi-record operating system, not the whole issuer balance sheet. · Clock: Application evidence and operating controls are proposed; no named stack has passed review. · Watch: Named key holders, supply controls, reconciliation frequency, breaks and examiner access.

Rule: Issuer-paid interest or yield for holding, using or retaining a stablecoin is prohibited; specified issuer-funded affiliate, service-provider and white-label paths face a rebuttable presumption. · Effect: Brings contracts, funding flows, branding and reward economics at distribution partners into the issuer perimeter. · Clock: Proposed related-party and rebuttal tests; not a final judgment on every independent reward program. · Watch: Final related-party definition, rebuttal evidence, distributor agreements and funding source.

Rule: Direct redemption would begin at one coin and generally finish within two business days, subject to onboarding, bounded safe harbors and regulator-imposed emergency limits. · Effect: Separates issuer redemption, reserve monetization and external wallet/exchange/bank settlement clocks. · Clock: Proposed service clock; no universal secondary-market par guarantee or end-to-end payout clock. · Watch: Final holder right, fees, onboarding, liquidity buffers, redemption incidents and cash-settlement receipts.
How is supply created, distributed, reconciled and redeemed?
Connect mint/burn authority and issuer books to distribution contracts, direct redemption and external settlement.

rows.title: Operations and proof
fields: Rule: Governance must cover smart contracts, private keys, cyber, privacy, continuity, third parties, AML/CFT, sanctions, transaction processing and records. · Effect: Turns networks, oracles, bridges, wallets and vendors into accountable dependencies with change, incident and recovery controls. · Clock: Proposed controls; an enterprise parent framework does not erase PPSI-specific accountability. · Watch: Final control standards, service-provider contracts, recovery tests, incidents and supervisory findings.

Rule: Monthly examined reserve reports, executive certifications, confidential weekly operating data, public quarterly financials and periodic full-scope examinations would expose the operating body. · Effect: Creates distinct public, supervisory and examiner-access data planes, including access to DLT records. · Clock: Proposed reporting/exam regime; 18-to-36-month exam discretion depends on specified conditions. · Watch: Final forms, first filings, auditor criteria, examination cycle and publication quality.
Which controls keep the system inspectable and recoverable?
Bind governance, smart contracts, keys, vendors, cyber, privacy, continuity, financial crime, public reports and examiner access.

rows.title: Capital and loss
fields: Rule: Capital combines tangible equity, reserve credit-risk charges, graduated issuance scale, non-reserve revenue and a realized-loss scalar with remediation powers. · Effect: Links reserve counterparties, operating scale, service businesses and historical losses to a separate loss-absorbing buffer. · Clock: All percentages and scalar parameters remain proposed. · Watch: Final calibration, eligible capital, look-through methods, loss data and remediation orders.
Which buffer absorbs reserve credit and operating loss?
Keep tangible equity, reserve credit charges, issuance scale, non-reserve revenue, loss history and remediation distinct.

rows.title: Parent, state and emergency seams
fields: Rule: Parent-bank capital would deconsolidate the PPSI and deduct its minimum from CET1; state issuers retain ordinary state supervision with extraordinary Board backup and a separate large-issuer transition lane. · Effect: Separates subsidiary loss absorption, parent exposure, state supervision and emergency infrastructure failure. · Clock: Proposed capital, enforcement and transition mechanics; no state issuer is converted by this release. · Watch: Final rule, state certification/equivalence, waiver decisions, first examination and emergency action.
Where do subsidiary, parent, state and Board responsibility meet?
Track parent CET1, ordinary state supervision, extraordinary Board backup, transition waivers and infrastructure-failure indicators.

rows.title: What the Fed's GENIUS proposals change in the crypto stack
fields: Label: Issuer / application interface · Meaning: The governed ecosystem contains a payment-stablecoin issuer or issuer-like operating surface that would face the proposal directly if the exact legal entity enters the Board-supervised lane. This is not an eligibility or approval finding.

Label: Custody / distribution interface · Meaning: The ecosystem supplies custody, distribution, market, cash or payout functions that the issuer would have to map and control, without becoming the issuer merely by providing them.

Label: Technical control interface · Meaning: The ecosystem can carry token state, contracts, data or interoperability and would be tested as an operational dependency, not as the legal source of issuer authority or reserve eligibility.

Label: Outside direct issuer perimeter · Meaning: The tracked object is primarily a different asset, market or institutional function. It may connect to the stack, but the proposal does not directly convert it into a payment-stablecoin issuer or reserve.
Twenty governed ecosystems mapped against twelve proposed issuer, reserve, custody, redemption, reporting, capital and application gates.

The two Board proposals define a possible federal issuer operating constitution and an insured-state-member-bank application path. They regulate legal entities, claims, assets, controls, books and clocks; they do not approve a technology stack. The matrix shows which current Hub surface would be directly tested, used as a regulated service interface, treated as a technical dependency, or remain outside the direct issuer perimeter.

Every row is a proposal-overlap finding only. It does not establish that an ecosystem is a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, an eligible reserve asset, an approved custodian, a Board-approved subsidiary, compliant with a final rule or operating in a Board-supervised lane.

fields: Read each lane as a different legal relationship around the same issuer. Repeated appearances of the issuer do not create multiple issuers; they show that one legal person carries several distinct obligations.
